chunks: Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā, from Mūsā ibn ʿUmar, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mughīrah, from Abī al-Ṣabbāḥ al-Muzanī, who said:
Amīr al-Muʾminīn عليه السلام: There are ninety-five takbīrs in the day and night for the prayers; among them is the takbīr of the qunūt.

Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan said: These narrations that we have mentioned are those upon which practice should be based, and according to them our Shaykh al-Mufīd, may Allah have mercy on him, used to give fatwa formerly. Then, near the end of his life, he came to abandon acting upon them and adopted acting upon raising the hands without takbīr. The first view is more appropriate due to the existence of the narrations concerning it, and besides this I do not know of any hadith at all.

And it is not for anyone to interpret these reports by saying: What exceeds ninety takbīrs, I take to mean that when he rises from the first tashahhud to the third rakʿah, he rises with a takbīr—for several reasons:

One of them is that reports are only interpreted away from their apparent meanings, and their outward sense left, when they conflict and some of them oppose others. Here, there is nothing that opposes these narrations, so it is not permissible to turn away from their apparent meanings by any kind of interpretation.

The second is that not all prayers contain a rising from the second rakʿah to the third; rather, that is found only in four prayers. If that were what was meant, then it would have said: ninety-four takbīrs.

The third is that the detailed hadith includes mention of eleven takbīrs in the dawn prayer, and a takbīr after that for the qunūt added to them. If the matter were as interpreted in that way, then the takbīr in it would have been only eleven takbīrs.

The fourth is that separate narrations have been transmitted stating that a person should rise from the first tashahhud to the third rakʿah and say: “By the power of Allah and His strength I rise and sit,” and they did not mention the takbīr. If rising with takbīr had been obligatory, then it would have said: “Then he says takbīr and rises to the third,” just as, when they mentioned bowing and prostration, they said: “Then he says takbīr and bows,” and “he says takbīr and prostrates,” and “he raises his head from prostration and says takbīr.” So if there had been a takbīr here, it would have said the like of that.

key_terms.التَّأْوِيلِ: Interpretive re-reading away from the outward meaning of the reports.
key_terms.التَّشَهُّدِ: The seated testimony in prayer after which one may rise to the next rakʿah.
key_terms.الرِّوَايَاتُ: The transmitted reports used as the basis for legal practice and argumentation.
key_terms.الصَّلَوَاتِ: The prescribed daily prayers under discussion in the narration.
key_terms.الْقُنُوتِ: The supplicatory act in prayer for which a takbīr is here counted.
key_terms.تَكْبِيرَةً: A declaration of 'Allāhu akbar' counted within the movements and acts of prayer.
key_terms.صَلَاةِ الْغَدَاةِ: The dawn prayer, cited specifically in counting the takbīrs.
key_terms.ظَوَاهِرِهَا: The apparent meanings of the narrations, which are argued to be binding absent contradiction.

ai.seo_question: Is there a takbīr for qunūt in the five daily prayers, and should rising to the third rakʿah be done with takbīr?
ai.summary: This hadith and the accompanying discussion address the number of takbīrs in the daily prayers, affirming that the takbīr for qunūt is included in the total. The passage then argues, on hadith-methodological and legal grounds, against reinterpreting the reports to make the extra takbīr refer to rising for the third rakʿah after the first tashahhud.
